content:
While people may try in earnest, no one in Kentucky can really pinpoint with certitude the end of the summer season and the beginning of autumn. The people who do often gesture vaguely to the arrival of pumpkin spice and Keeneland. Under no circumstances should their opinions carry any weight. Thankfully for those who don’t even bother to partake in this exercise, this Grenache Blanc from Ridge Vineyards shows up in a quantum state of living both seasons at once. Kind of like a guy wearing cargo shorts, an undersized soccer jersey picked up on clearance and sandals to Christmas dinner, oblivious to the world around him.

It’s a blend of 85% Grenache Blanc, 12% Picpoul, and 3% Roussanne and presents with aromas of pear, orange zest and mild jasmine. However, it’s on the palate where this wine spreads out with ample generosity: plenty of pear joined by ripe apricot, hazelnut, and a big current of minerality on the finish with enough acidity to keep things well focused throughout.

What you end up with is a wine built for the tail end of a long patio dinner, and it’s the first evening you notice you needed a sweatshirt or sweater and failed to bring one along. It doesn’t rush things, and when it comes to enjoying this bottle, nor should you. It already knows where the calendar is going and works well in either season with measured restraint and class.

A- / $43

title: Review: Shang Whiskey Dan Ya and East + West Kentucky Blend

content:
It’s not every day we get to sample an entirely new category of spirits. But that’s very much what Shang Whiskey is selling, with two launch offerings built around a whiskey distilled from Chinese baijiu.

The first — Dàn Ya — is redistilled from sauce-aroma (jiàngxiang) baijiu, which is produced from red sorghum. The redistilled spirit is then sent to Kentucky, where it is aged for under a year in American oak. It’s a fusion of Chinese and American production techniques, original enough that Shang is promoting it as a new category unto itself: jiàngxiang whiskey.

Shang’s second expression — the East + West Kentucky Blend — begins with the same jiàngxiang whiskey base. It’s blended with a Kentucky-distilled red sorghum whiskey, then aged in American oak before bottling.

Almost as notable as the production methods are the array of players involved in bringing the new spirits to market. Shang is owned by Maritine Brands, itself a joint venture between True Essence Foods and Guìzhou Guótái Shùzhì Liquor Group. Further partners include Whiskey House of Kentucky (in Elizabethtown) and The Blending House (in Shelbyville).

It’s a unique approach to melding distinct spirits categories and styles. And while many Westerners are still unfamiliar with baijiu, it’s generally considered the world’s largest spirits category, with annual sales almost double that of the global whiskey market. At the outset, Shang seems keen on targeting two separate consumer bases: baijiu-curious Americans, and existing baijiu drinkers searching for an injection of novelty.

Let’s dive in.

Shang Whiskey Dàn Ya Review

The baijiu used for Dàn Ya’s jiàngxiang whiskey begins with red sorghum in the Chìshui River basin. The sorghum base undergoes solid-state fermentation using dàqu, a starter that facilitates both saccharification and fermentation. Production follows a complex series of eight fermentations, separated by seven distillations. The distillate is rested in oxygen permeable clay pots for a minimum of three years. Finally, the baijiu is pot distilled and pressure filtered before shipping to Kentucky, where the resulting jiàngxiang whiskey is aged in American oak for between one month to “just under” a year.

On the nose, dedicated whiskey drinkers will likely encounter something quite new. Early aromas are at once tangy, sour, fruity, floral, and salty, somewhere between overripe tropical fruit and a savory fermented sauce or bean paste. Additional notes include bitter melon, lemongrass, pickled watermelon rind, and unsweetened chocolate. It’s certainly a broad mix, and it takes time to really parse the individual components. Oak develops later on, lending touches of vanilla and light caramel, which (eventually) push the nose into more familiar whiskey territory.

The palate starts with floral simple syrup and a big hit of red peppercorns, the latter dominating for a couple sips. After some acclimation comes loads more fruit, including tart berry compote, passionfruit, lychee, and pomelo. The back palate brings salinity and sweet/savory red bean paste, with lingering pepper. 100 proof.

B+ / $65 (500ml)

Shang Whiskey East + West Kentucky Blend Review

East + West starts with the jiàngxiang whiskey base and marries it with whiskey distilled from 100% red sorghum. That second component is produced at Whiskey House via sweet mash fermentation and grain-on column distillation up to 155 proof. (A Whiskey House representative confirmed the team used a relatively neutral yeast and enzymes similar to a high corn bourbon.) After the two components are blended, they undergo maturation in American oak barrels.

East + West kicks off with a profile far more familiar to whiskey drinkers. The nose begins with toasted oak and fermenting grain, and at first, it’s a little reminiscent of fermenting mash. Baking spice and chocolate are up next, and once again, it’s still firmly in whiskey territory: allspice, clove, and nutmeg meet hot cocoa. Eventually, some of the funky, ripe fruit character from Dàn Ya rolls in, along with a savory, peppery sauce (hoisin comes to mind).

The palate borrows a lot from Dàn Ya, with both pepper and tart fruit dialed back by around half. That allows for more caramel and milk chocolate, along with threads of bright red cherry and honeydew I didn’t pick up on the first expression. Similarly, the saline is toned down, and in its place we’ve got both pickled and candied ginger. The sweeter finish brings golden raisins and black pepper.

For American palates, East + West is less adventurous but more familiar. My guess is that could up the appeal stateside, though it reigns in some of what makes Dàn Ya intricate and fun. 92 proof.

B+ / $46 (500ml)

title: Review: Angostura Demerara Sugar Syrup and Spicy Honey Syrup
summary:

The post Review: Angostura Demerara Sugar Syrup and Spicy Honey Syrup appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
When it comes to cocktails, everyone knows Angostura for their iconic bitters. Now the brand is branching out into the cocktail syrup game with the introduction of their new Demerara Sugar Syrup and Spicy Honey Syrup. Cocktail syrups can be great for simplifying cocktail preparation at home, but they can also be tricky, sometimes packing too much flavor and sweetness to the point that they overpower a standard base spirit. Let’s check out this duo from Angostura and see if they nailed the formulas out of the gate.

Angostura Demerara Sugar Syrup Review

The Demerara Sugar Syrup is the more versatile of the two, something you can use for almost any cocktail built around a barrel-aged spirit like whiskey or rum. It’s rich without being overly thick, delivering bold notes of overcooked caramel, molasses, and toffee that immediately distinguish it from standard simple syrup. But go easy because things can get overly saccharine fast if you’re not careful. Added sparingly, it contributes a nice mix of sweetness and texture to cocktails. The Old Fashioned recipe printed on the label is a good example, recommending half an ounce of syrup to two ounces of bourbon. If that bourbon is 100 proof or higher, you might be alright, but it’s simply too sweet with a standard 80-90 proof bottle. Start with a quarter of an ounce and work your way up, and the syrup adds that richness without overwhelming the whiskey. B+

Angostura Spicy Honey Syrup Review

The Spicy Honey Syrup is the more adventurous of the two, but also the more restrained when it comes to sweetness. Built on a foundation of floral honey, it layers warming baking spices, cinnamon, clove, and a touch of peppery heat into a syrup that feels equally suited to whiskey, rum, tequila, and even non-alcoholic cocktails. The spice isn’t overblown, but it does lend a noticeable, red chili warmth that lingers. It shines in a Gold Rush, a Hot Toddy, or, as Angostura recommends on the label, a spicy margarita. The honey softens the citrus and adds a silky texture while the spice infuses a gentle, complimenting heat. Another pro tip: you may need to look for added sweetness in other ingredients when using this syrup. Classic bourbons work well enough, but in a margarita, you’ll need a sweeter tequila (I’d use a reposado) or a dash of triple sec to achieve balance. B+

Like their iconic bitters, Angostura’s new syrups are no instant cocktail shortcut, but used thoughtfully and judiciously, they enhance all manner of drinks and should save bartenders, professional and novice alike, a few steps behind the bar.

$12 each (375ml)

content:
When the Isle of Harris Distillery opened in 2015, it wasn’t simply launching another Scotch whisky brand. It was attempting something far more ambitious: creating meaningful work in one of Scotland’s most remote communities and proving that world-class spirits could emerge from the edge of the Atlantic. There was just one issue. Almost no one involved had ever made spirits before.

The distillery’s original employees—known locally as the “Tarbert Ten”—came not from the whisky industry but from careers in construction and hospitality, among others. Together, they learned the craft of spirits production from the ground up, building both a distillery and a culture defined by curiosity and experimentation. That spirit of continual learning remains central to the Isle of Harris story today.

Few people embody that journey better than Shona Macleod. A member of the founding team, she joined as Guest Services Manager before discovering an unexpected talent for sensory analysis and blending, helping to make Isle of Harris Gin before shifting to whisky production and, in 2023, becoming official distillery blender. In her current role, she has guided the release of a line of young single malts including their newest addition, Isle of Harris Whisky.

In our conversation, Macleod discusses the challenges of distilling on a remote island, what makes Isle of Harris whiskies unique, and how a distillery founded to support the island’s community is now working with other Hebridean distilleries to bring that region’s unique whiskies to the world.

Note: This interview has been edited for clarity.

Drinkhacker: What is your background in spirits production? How did you become the official blender at the Isle of Harris Distillery?

Macleod: In December 2014, I joined the distillery as part of the “Tarbert Ten” and began my journey as Guest Services Manager. Our original small team were all involved in gin quality from the very beginning and we were tested to check if we had good sensory skills. It had never crossed my mind that I did or that it would be something I would enjoy but I did!  My involvement in the sensory and quality aspects of Isle of Harris Gin then naturally sparked a deep interest in whisky production and flavour profiles in both new make spirit and maturing whisky.

As we moved closer to launching our first whisky, we needed more in-house expertise in sensory work and blending, so I began a new chapter within the production team.   Learning the craft and science of distillation, maturation, and cask selection has been a huge learning curve for me.  Every day brings new opportunities, challenges, and the joy of creating something that reflects our island home.

Drinkhacker: I’ve read that there is an “always learning” mindset at the distillery. How has that been applied in your whisky-making?

Macleod: It’s quite an appropriate phrase when it comes to our whisky making as the distillery is only 10 years old, and we were all new to whisky making when we started out. The purpose of the distillery was to create jobs locally, as such, the company had to recruit people who lived on the island. With no history of distilling here in Harris, these roles were filled by a group of people who had no previous experience in the whisky industry. Our original distillers came from different backgrounds such as facilities management, engineering and the building trade. It was a big learning curve for all involved so we are always learning!

Drinkhacker: How has the distillery supported the broader community on Isle of Harris?

Macleod: The purpose of the distillery extends beyond making whisky and gin. Primarily by providing employment and career development opportunities in a small community and sustaining many families. It has helped keep some young locals on the island who may have gone elsewhere to follow a career path. Instead, they found interesting opportunities here. To others like myself with no experience in the whisky industry, it offered a new challenge and something for us to be proud of. The ability for many of us to live and work at home in Harris has had a really positive economic impact on the island.

More broadly, the aim was also to help boost tourism and be a catalyst for other small businesses to develop and make Harris a better destination for visitors. We have welcomed over 650,000 visitors through our doors since opening in September 2015 which is quite exceptional.

Drinkhacker: What are some of the challenges of producing single malt whisky on an island like Harris?

Macleod: Building a new business in a remote location is a challenge in itself in terms of logistics, infrastructure and added costs for almost everything.  From finding a suitable site with a fresh water source nearby through to the construction phase and all the challenges that brought wasn’t easy by any means. Specialist firms had to be used to construct the distilling plant, and the ongoing maintenance is costly as people have to travel from the mainland and stay over when work is being carried out if it can’t be handled locally. We rely on ferries to take all our raw materials in and finished goods away which can be challenging when we’re at the mercy of the Hebridean weather! We’re no strangers to shifting schedules and thinking on our feet.

Drinkhacker: How would you describe the Isle of Harris house whisky style? What sets it apart from whiskies from other regions of Scotland?

Macleod: It’s unique because it’s the first whisky from the Isle of Harris, at least the first legal one. I’m sure there were illicit stills many years ago! We set up our production processes to produce a certain type of new make spirit, one that was light and fruity and quick to mature but as no one had produced whisky commercially here before, we didn’t know how long it might take to be at its best, ready for release. Happily, we discovered that the maturation conditions are excellent at our warehouses on the shores of the Atlantic and within five years we had a good idea that we had something special.

In terms of style, there isn’t a ‘Hebridean’ style as such, so we weren’t aiming to produce a whisky that was particularly like any other in flavour profile. Instead, we set out to create a dram of distinction, fruity, floral and spiced with just a touch of smoke. The most important thing was that it was complex and full of character, just like the people making it.

Drinkhacker: What is unique about your production process?

Macleod: Our process is not hurried by time, everything is fairly slow such as the mash, the fermentations and the distillation time. Our distillers are involved with every part of the process, it’s not automated so they manually adjust steam valves and the cut point is made using sight and nosing skills. I think the human touch influences the character and quality of the spirit and importantly gives them real skills in the art of distilling that they might not have learnt in a larger distillery.

Drinkhacker: What is wood management like on the island? How did you settle on oloroso and Fino in addition to ex-bourbon for aging your whiskies?
Macleod: Cask availability is much the same as anywhere else, they just have to travel a little further to reach us! Some from Kentucky and some from Southern Spain. Our casks are delivered straight into the yard at the distillery, next to the shore at East Loch Tarbert where they sit until they’re filled before being sent to the maturation warehouses, 2 miles from the distillery. I’ve no doubt the proximity to the sea prior to filling helps add a maritime character to the whisky as it ages.

The original cask mix of ex bourbon barrels from Buffalo Trace, Heaven Hill and Woodford Reserve, plus ex oloroso casks was decided on during the development phase when we had experienced consultants to help with recipes and production processes. Fino came a little later as a bit of an experiment, but we discovered that Fino casks mature our spirit really well in this climate.  In addition to our core cask portfolio, we have a small number of sweet wine casks from our friends at Chateau Biac in Bordeaux, Pennsylvanian Rye casks from Dad’s Hat Distillery, Pedro Ximenez, Palo Cortado and Orange Wine casks from our Spanish supplier, Yose y Miguel Martin in Heulva.

Drinkhacker: What is the maturation climate like on the island?

Macleod: We have quite stable temperatures through the year in The Hebrides, it never gets too hot or too cold which is an ideal atmosphere for whisky maturation.  The Island is directly on the Atlantic so there is always a lot of moisture in the air from frequent rainfall and sea mist, this humidity seems to aid maturation. It’s often very windy where the warehouses are located. This can encourage the angels share to disappear a little quicker, but it produces some great whisky in a relatively short period of time.

Drinkhacker: Other distilleries are following your lead in the Outer Hebrides. Are you working together?

Macleod: In 2018 we began to develop “The Hebridean Whisky Trail” with neighboring distilleries on the Isle of Skye – Raasay, Torabhaig and Talisker. Our aim was to put a spotlight on this part of The Hebrides as a whisky destination and a producer of world class spirits. With three of the four of us being new (Talisker pre-dated the rest of us by about 180 years!) it was always hoped that other Outer Hebridean Distilleries would emerge which they did in the years that followed. On the neighbouring island of Benbecula, North Uist Distillery and Benbecula Distillery have been established and joined the trail. It’s been fantastic to see new distilleries open up close by and welcomed with open arms. In addition, our friends from Tiree Distillery and Tobermory have also joined. Each year we have our own Hebridean Whisky Festival in September involving all the distilleries which continues to grow from strength to strength. Perhaps we’ll be granted an official region title one day, that’s our hope.


Drinkhacker: How does the new Isle of Harris Whisky fit into the brand’s portfolio?

Macleod: It represents a natural next step for the distillery, moving from a single flagship whisky to a broader range and builds our portfolio. With more maturing stock available, It’s an evolution rather than a change of direction. We want this dram to be seen as one to enjoy with friends and family rather than being viewed as a collectible whisky or one saved for special occasions. It’s really versatile so it can be enjoyed as a traditional straight dram or used in highballs and cocktails. Please try it and let me know what you think!

Drinkhacker: After a decade of whisky-making, what are you most proud of?

Macleod: I’m very proud to see the growth that the distillery has enjoyed and how much we’ve achieved in the past 10 years. Building an international award-winning brand from our small island in the Outer Hebrides, creating skilled jobs and marking our place in the history books are highlights for me personally.  The success of Isle of Harris Gin is ongoing and to now have three core whiskies on the market that we are truly proud of is a real milestone for us.

Drinkhacker: What will the distillery look like in another decade? What do you hope to achieve going forward?

Macleod: No one knows what the future holds, but we’ll strive to continue to produce world class spirits from Harris and look forward to continued growth. To build on the success of the first 10 years and to always remember the vision that our founder Anderson Bakewell had in those early years when he wondered to himself “how can we bottle the essence of this beautiful island and share it with the world”.

content:
When we last visited Glenglassaugh’s core range in 2023, the final scores threw a curveball. The distillery’s 12 year old single malt — the line’s only age-stated whisky — lagged behind the NAS bottlings. (We also reviewed a 46 year from before the distillery’s 1986 shuttering, which is a different and altogether great whisky.) But 2026 brings a range expansion, and with it, a chance to reassess. Glenglassaugh 15 Years Old is the newest permanent expression from the Highlands distillery, and the first to leverage Pedro Ximénez sherry for aging.

Blending was overseen by Dr. Rachel Barrie, who serves as Master Blender for Glenglassaugh and sister distilleries Glendronach and Benriach. (All three are owned by Louisville-based Brown-Forman.) The whisky was aged across both PX sherry and Spanish wine casks, which Barries says adds an “indulgent depth of flavor” to Glenglassaugh’s typically coastal and fruity profile.

Let’s dive in.

Glenglassaugh 15 Years Old Review

Pedro Ximénez influence is front and center on the nose, with alternating waves of dates, brandied cherries, and black raisins. Burnt orange peel lends a touch of citrus, but it pales in comparison to those dark, dried fruits. A dry nuttiness is up next, closest to black walnut, along with a less pronounced thread of toasted sesame oil. Toffee, roasted coffee beans, and cocoa powder round out a nose reminiscent of whiskies from sister distillery Glendronach — and quite unlike any other whiskies in the standard Glenglassaugh lineup.

Based on the nose, I was worried the 15 year’s palate could turn into a sherry bomb. Fortunately, that influence is a tad less declarative here, allowing the distillate itself to shine on first sips. Hallmark tropical and orchard fruits hit early, including guava, apple juice, and very ripe papaya, drizzled with a dark syrup or treacle. Overall, the fruits aren’t quite as bright as with some other Glenglassaugh malts (like Sandend), and they’re tempered by PX and oxidized wine; still, the end result is a pleasantly sweet, somewhat richer medley. Chocolate arrives only at and beyond the midpalate, far lighter than the nose, along with tart marmalade.

The finish gradually transitions from fruit, treacle, and chocolate to sweetened espresso. (A nice Café Cubano, if you want to get fancy.) A touch of lingering salinity continues for well over a minute after each sip — appropriate for a famously coastal aging setup.

It’s a nice bookend to the narrative, one that very much feels like Glenglassaugh through the eyes of Rachel Barrie. I’ll admit that when I first heard the whisky’s specs — specifically the use of Pedro Ximénez — I was a bit skeptical. But Barrie lands the plane. Glenglassaugh 15 Years Old improves on the distillery’s 12 year bottling by tempering the graininess and introducing significantly more depth from the casks. Fingers crossed we see more in this direction.

92 proof.

A- / $110

The post Tasting Report: Spotlight on 2026 Italian Wine Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We didn’t make it to Wine Paris this year, but Wine Paris made it to us, courtesy of Communicare il Vino, which sent along 12 selections from its Italian portfolio which were showcased at the event. These hail from all over Italy, and we’re breaking them down by broad category, then order of preference.

Sparkling

2025 Sant’Anna dei Bricchetti Vino Spumante Incanto Pas Dosè – Rather dry and initially innocuous, the wine opens up with time to reveal a core of lemon and melon, though it’s all rather buried under a heavy layer of doughy yeast. An initially intense fizz takes some time to settle down, but it takes a lot of that fruit with it. B / $17

Whites

2023 Rosset Petite Arvine Valle d’Aoste – Petite arvine is a white grape varietal designed to thrive in cold climates. This unoaked offering showcases a mix of honeysuckle and fresh fruit, namely apple and aromatic pear notes, with touches of Meyer lemon. Lightly perfumed as the finish builds, notes of sandalwood give it a slightly smoldering vibe that hints at incense. Outstanding as an aperitif. A- / $35

2022 Querceto di Castellina Livia IGT – A quirky blend of viognier and roussanne, two grapes I rarely associate with Italy at all. The more Rhone-leaning side of this blend dominates here, offering a floral-herbal character that emerges as quite dry and pastoral. Elements of hay and lemongrass give the finish a massive length, but one that plays in the forest and the dust, merely tiptoeing into the orchard to grab a fig or an apricot from time to time. B+ / $45

2024 La Regola Steccaia IGT – Vermentino doesn’t often acquit itself as this gentle and supple, layers of nougat and pastry cream evoking notes of melon, covered in white flowers. A sharper, zippier note hints at the heavy acidity that vermentino is so well-known for, but it never breaks out of its more undulating groove, concluding on notes of coconut cream. A light grind of lemon peel across the top finishes things out on a lighter note. B+ / $40

Reds

2023 Sassotondo Monte Calvo Ciliegiolo – There are a few Monte Calvos in Italy; this one is a small volcano in Tuscany’s Maremma region, where ciliegiolo grapes (purportedly a progenitor of sangiovese, though this is disputed) grow in the volcanic soil. Aged in large barrels for a year, this wine is a delight. Light on its feet, this effortless expression of the grape showcases cherry fruit at its brightest and most maraschino-like, gently sweet and layered with light notes of almond syrup, red flowers, and a pinch of peppery spice. Its flavors are beautifully integrated from start to finish, culminating in a seductive creaminess you don’t often find in a wine the light in body. Delightful. A / $45

2024 San Gregorio Chianti Colli Senesi (pictured) – Bright berries kick things off with a rush of cherry, followed by some surprising blueberry notes, all swirled together with cinnamon syrup. Light notes of graphite and tar add just enough tannic gravity to the wine, which finishes a bit on the tart side with a punch of fresh cranberry juice. This gentle sourness becomes more insistent as the wine fades, but it maintains a lively balance throughout that invites repeated visits. A shockingly good value. A / $15

2021 Ricordi Sant’Anna dei Bricchetti Barbera d’Asti DOCG – A bolder and denser barbera than you’re likely to encounter in the wild, this is a rich and more fruit-forward experience that shocks as it evokes barbera’s big brother grapes far more than expected. Unctuous notes of plum and cherry meld with black tea and bittersweet chocolate, but ample acidity linger throughout the experience — well into the finish. Tart boysenberry and spice elements give the conclusion a holiday feel that, again, doesn’t connect with the classic barbera experience — but which isn’t at all unwelcome. A- / $10

2021 Capezzana Ghiaie della Furba IGT – An unusual super Tuscan blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, and Merlot, this is one of the more intense and brooding wines I’ve encountered in recent memory, overloaded with tar and turned earth, punctuated throughout with anise. Dark chocolate, coffee bean, and blackstrap molasses notes meld fitfully as the palate develops, culminating in rich, impossibly black fruit overtones that somehow get more intense as the wine develops. Let this monster linger in the cellar for another decade and you are likely to be rewarded with a lithe experience that shows Tuscany at the top of its game. Ands yet, surprisingly, it’s still approachable now, as long as you are prepared for what you’re getting in to. A- / $70

2021 Monchiero Barolo Rocche di Castiglione DOCG – Amazingly floral on the nose, infused with roses that telegraph where this wine might end up, but the palate is tight as a fist for now. Airtime or decanting is a help, tempering tannins and the more balsamic elements of the wine, revealing a layer of turned earth waiting underneath. Bright cherry emerges after that, although slightly underripe, a further sign of how many years this wine has ahead of it. There’s joy to be had now with ample patience, but I’d likely try it again around 2031. B+/ $64

2019 Pardi Montefalco Rosso Riserva DOC – Intense cherry backed with rhubarb kicks things off on this intense yet approachable wine, which fades slowly into notes of plum, bittersweet chocolate, and rum raisin elements. Brooding with green herbs and turned earth as the finish approaches, a slightly leathery character awaits as the finish approaches. The experience remains tart to an extreme, with licks of anise ringing the edges of the wine. Ideally paired with a lively dinner. B+ / $27

2018 Antonelli Chiusa di Pannone Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG – A well-aged sagrantino, this wine hits hard with notes of raisin and dried currants, increasingly tarry as it develops in glass. The tannins remain firm to the point of being nearly overbearing, giving the back end a heavy character of tar and asphalt, somewhat bitter at times. The finish echoes blackberry and prune notes, with dark chocolate making a brief appearance. Though aggressive, this could be an interesting choice today with the right meal pairing, but something that probably needs 5 to 10 more years in cellar to develop. B+ / $57

2022 Castello La Leccia Chianti Classico – Quite dry on the attack, with a balsamic edge and overtones of turned earth, anise, and late-stage basil. Graphite and slate inform an enduringly bone-dry palate that sees some dried florals developing but which never quite come to fruition. Cherry fruit on the finish is rather underripe, laced with tar and pencil lead. B / $20

title: Review: Pride of Anderson County Bourbon 9.5 Years Old
summary:

The post Review: Pride of Anderson County Bourbon 9.5 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Rare Character Whiskey launched in 2021, founded by spirits industry veterans Pablo Moix and Peter Nevenglosky. The independent bottler quickly developed a devoted following by focusing on single barrel selections, custom labels, and premium whiskey stocks. It also became closely associated with its barrel code system, with certain codes developing dedicated followings and becoming highly collectible.

In the spring of 2023, Rare Character temporarily shifted its focus away from barrel code branding for Pride of Anderson County Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey. The original release left little room for speculation about its origin. The back label identified Wild Turkey Distilling in Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, as the source of the bourbon while also specifying the rickhouse and floor where each barrel matured. It even referenced Tyrone, Kentucky, the small unincorporated riverfront community in Anderson County located roughly three miles from Lawrenceburg and generally regarded as the more precise location of Wild Turkey. Enthusiasm surrounding the inaugural release was considerable, and bottles quickly became difficult to obtain.

Three years later, Rare Character introduced the next chapter for Pride of Anderson County. The brand shifted from a lottery-exclusive release to an ongoing single barrel series. Although the name remains Pride of Anderson County, the back label received a significant overhaul. The 2026 version omits any reference to Wild Turkey, its rickhouses, individual warehouse floors, or Tyrone.

Rare Character was unable to comment on the source of the 2026 iterations of Pride of Anderson County due to non-disclosure agreements. Even so, the origins of the brand remain closely tied to Wild Turkey, and Anderson County is home to the distillery. With almost full certainty, Pride of Anderson County continues to be distilled by Wild Turkey from a mashbill of 75% corn, 13% rye, and 12% malted barley, using entirely non-GMO grains. Pride of Anderson County is aged for at least nine years in barrels with a #4 alligator char and entered into the barrel at 115 proof after the distillate exits the column still at 125 proof and the doubler at 128 proof.

Rare Character provided Drinkhacker with a review sample aged for at least 9.5 years, making it several years younger than the 13.5 year-old bourbon released in 2023. According to Rare Character, Pride of Anderson County is intended as “a tribute to legends… both past and present.”

Does the liquid live up to the legend?

Pride of Anderson County Bourbon 9.5 Years Old Review

The nose opens with an artificial vanilla taffy note that arrives with plenty of intensity but disappears almost as quickly as it appears. From there, dried cherries and sweetened cocoa powder take over, while roasted pecans arrive later to provide a sturdy foundation along with a touch of tannic dryness. Aside from that fleeting vanilla note at the start, the bouquet lands squarely in classic bourbon territory.

The palate begins with sweet apple jelly before shifting into a potent, short-lived sour cherry note. That quickly transforms into cherry cola, accompanied by a medium-thick mouthfeel. The finish keeps the cherry theme going with cherry preserves and dark brown sugar. That darker sweetness transitions into a smidge of sweet and nutty late-harvest dark maple syrup before closing with sweet cinnamon chewing gum.

This is a fun bourbon. Beyond the opening aroma of artificial vanilla, Pride of Anderson County delivers on nearly every front. For anyone seeking a bourbon driven by cherry, this bottle fits the bill. I cannot recall another bourbon that explores so many different expressions of cherry within a single pour, and I enjoyed every minute of that ride. With that said, as much as I enjoyed this bourbon, the asking price of $250 is a tall ask. If this specific barrel were priced in the range of $150, I’d be all in.

119.8 proof.

A / $250

The post Review: Tequilas of House of Rare appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
House of Rare is a tequila initiative that got its start with a particular mission: Rather than focusing on tradition, the operation is focused on sourcing unusual and rare casks to finish its spirits, releasing them as limited editions and collaborations. (Tawny Port finish, anyone? Umeshu?)

As well, recently the brand began releasing its own distillate as a standard blanco without any fancy finishing and as a reposado, aged in PX sherry casks for six months. Both are produced at the Herencia de Agaves distillery in the El Arenal appellation of Jalisco.

We sampled three products from House of Rare, and we’ll add to this review as more arrive for tasting.

All reviewed here are NOM 1648.

House of Rare Tequila House Blanco Review

Agave-forward, almost to an extreme. This aggressive spirit pours on the pepper in both white and black formats. To call this vegetal would be an understatement, as the experience positively smolders with underbrush and notes of smudged sage. The palate is equally a bruiser, all pepper and barrel char, with greener agave notes just as pushy. A squeeze of lemon adds the only brighter note to the equation, along with some saline, but this is fleeting, as the finish returns to charrier, more brooding territory. If you really want to “taste the agave,” look no further. But complex it ain’t. 80 proof. B+ / $70

House of Rare Tequila Founder’s Cut Blanco Review

This limited edition blanco was the first release from House of Rare’s own distillery and was limited to 777 bottles. This is a milder but still intense tequila with many of the same trappings of the House Blanco, but cut on the nose with a touch of sweetness and some mint. The palate remains gravelly and rich, quite earthy and almost chocolatey at times. At the same time an industrial character clings to the experience, giving the finish a slightly off note. The lemon touches of the House Blanco are visible here, but instead they come across a bit closer to Lemon Pledge. More black pepper gives the conclusion an even more aggressive, lasting character. 80 proof. B+ / $180

House of Rare Tequila House Reposado Review

Aged in Pedro Ximenez sherry casks for 6 months. There’s no missing the sherry here, which effectively muscles out House of Rare’s more insistent agave notes to showcase a hugely nutty character, turning leathery and sharp, with smoldering torched citrus peel notes that evoke some smokiness as it develops. The palate acquits itself similarly, though with a bit more sweetness than expected, at least at first. Again that sherry takes over, becoming quite woody and tannic as it sits on the tongue. The finish sees some of the blanco’s more peppery and earthier elements coming into clearer focus, which is refreshing in that it adds something a little different to the wine-forward experience, but which muddies the experience more than I expected, leaving the fade-out more than a little scattered. 80 proof. B / $90

summary:

The post The Best Orange Bitters (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
After aromatic bitters, orange bitters are easily the most commonly called-for bittering agents in cocktails today. There’s also a huge variety of bitters available on the market. Are they any different? Which is best? I put four big bitters brands to the test to see which was best.

We’re updating this story with additional orange bitters brands as we receive them and have them ranked accordingly in the roundup.

Regans’ Orange Bitters No. 6 – A 1990s recreation of Charles Baker’s orange bitters recipe, brought to you by Gary Regan and the Sazerac Company. Tangerine notes on the nose, with clear notes of cardamom and clove-like character on the back end, dollowed by a hint of chocolate. Orange aplenty, but with a bracing, Fernet-like bitterness that really lingers, walloping you on the finish. The best of all worlds, packing both ample, authentic fruit and a big, bitter punch. 45% abv. A / $16 per 5 oz. bottle [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

Fee Brothers West Indian Orange Bitters – Very low alcohol. Lighter in color, much sweeter, but more orange-focused than Regan’s, offering sweet tangerine notes up front that fade into cinnamon and clove notes. Quite a bit sweeter than other brands, with an almost candylike edge to them — but I like the way they impart a clear orange character (along with mild bitterness) to a cocktail. I like these in punches and other party drinks but don’t reach for them for typical cocktailing needs. 9% abv. B+ / $12 per 4 oz. bottle [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

The Bitter Truth Orange Bitters – Interesting nose — light on orange and heavy on notes of coffee, roasted/smoked meat, ginger, and other savory elements. The body is a nice mix of citrus and more savory elements, but they aren’t overwhelmingly bitter. The smoky element is curious, but a bit at odds with the typical usage of orange bitters. 39% abv. B / $27 per 200ml bottle [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

Angostura Orange Bitters – Very pale in color, with a bright mandarin/tangerine note immediately evident. Very sweet on the palate, with a candylike quality that isn’t easily shaken. They’re very similar to Fee Brothers’ offering, except there’s not really any bitterness evident here at all. For a drop of orange candy in your drink, these are fine, but nuance is very much lacking. 28% abv. B / $13 per 4 oz. bottle [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

Warn Reserve Cocktail Co. Orange Bitters – An extremely bitter option in this category — perhaps the most bitter of them all — orange takes a distant back seat to overtones of gentian in the mix, giving this an almost fernet-like feel. While some orange peel arrives soon after tucking into the sip, it comes across as torched and more than a little harsh, finishing on notes of cloves and leathery tree bark. If you like Angostura’s aromatic bitters — but want them tinged just so with a hint of citrus, this may be worth a look — but I expect most imbibers will be looking for orange bitters that are more clearly orange-forward. 44.7% abv. B / $24 per 5 oz. bottle

content:
Palm Republic Rum is part of a new vanguard of rum brands looking to bring ultra-high quality spirits to the market at a reasonable price. The secret seems to be smart blending: Source high-grade barrels from various locales and put them together to create a sophisticated finished product. This brand happens to be co-founded by Eric Winter, star of TV’s The Rookie.

Palm Republic offers two expressions at present. We reviewed them both.

Palm Republic Silver Rum Review

A blend of rums distilled in Jamaica and the U.S. Virgin Islands. It’s not indicated on the packaging or website but I presume this is lightly aged rum that has been filtered back to clear. The results are impressive. The nose is fruity with big banana notes but still sharp enough to evoke its youth, almost peppery at times. Vanilla sneaks its way into view, tempered by a light graphite quality. The palate is less biting than the nose would indicate, that banana amplified into full ice cream mode, and hitting a brown sugar stride as things come to a conclusion. A solid little mixer that punches above expectations. 80 proof. A- / $45

Palm Republic Aged Rum Review

A much more aggressive rum, blending rums from Panama, Jamaica, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, all aged up to eight years in sherry casks. The sherry isn’t shy with this rum, giving the nose a nutty, citrusy overtone alongside a fairly grassy underbelly. Smoldering on the palate, that sherry continues to rumble and push the rest of the experience around, imbuing the rum with a massive body — and quite a bit of sweetness. The big brown sugar belly on this rum undercuts the sherry, giving it a bit of a candied orange character, the finish eventually turning more saccharine than expected. Tasted neat, I felt like this clung to my palate for half an hour or more. It’s still a rousing, lively rum — but it mixes better than it drinks on its own. 92 proof. B / $50

content:
While people may try in earnest, no one in Kentucky can really pinpoint with certitude the end of the summer season and the beginning of autumn. The people who do often gesture vaguely to the arrival of pumpkin spice and Keeneland. Under no circumstances should their opinions carry any weight. Thankfully for those who don’t even bother to partake in this exercise, this Grenache Blanc from Ridge Vineyards shows up in a quantum state of living both seasons at once. Kind of like a guy wearing cargo shorts, an undersized soccer jersey picked up on clearance and sandals to Christmas dinner, oblivious to the world around him.

It’s a blend of 85% Grenache Blanc, 12% Picpoul, and 3% Roussanne and presents with aromas of pear, orange zest and mild jasmine. However, it’s on the palate where this wine spreads out with ample generosity: plenty of pear joined by ripe apricot, hazelnut, and a big current of minerality on the finish with enough acidity to keep things well focused throughout.

What you end up with is a wine built for the tail end of a long patio dinner, and it’s the first evening you notice you needed a sweatshirt or sweater and failed to bring one along. It doesn’t rush things, and when it comes to enjoying this bottle, nor should you. It already knows where the calendar is going and works well in either season with measured restraint and class.

A- / $43

title: Review: Shang Whiskey Dan Ya and East + West Kentucky Blend
summary:
It’s not every day we get to sample an entirely new category of spirits. But that’s very much what Shang Whiskey is selling, with two launch offerings built around a whiskey distilled from Chinese baijiu. The first — Dàn Ya — is redistilled from sauce-aroma (jiàngxiang) baijiu, which is produced from red sorghum. The redistilled…

The post Review: Shang Whiskey Dan Ya and East + West Kentucky Blend appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
It’s not every day we get to sample an entirely new category of spirits. But that’s very much what Shang Whiskey is selling, with two launch offerings built around a whiskey distilled from Chinese baijiu.

The first — Dàn Ya — is redistilled from sauce-aroma (jiàngxiang) baijiu, which is produced from red sorghum. The redistilled spirit is then sent to Kentucky, where it is aged for under a year in American oak. It’s a fusion of Chinese and American production techniques, original enough that Shang is promoting it as a new category unto itself: jiàngxiang whiskey.

Shang’s second expression — the East + West Kentucky Blend — begins with the same jiàngxiang whiskey base. It’s blended with a Kentucky-distilled red sorghum whiskey, then aged in American oak before bottling.

Almost as notable as the production methods are the array of players involved in bringing the new spirits to market. Shang is owned by Maritine Brands, itself a joint venture between True Essence Foods and Guìzhou Guótái Shùzhì Liquor Group. Further partners include Whiskey House of Kentucky (in Elizabethtown) and The Blending House (in Shelbyville).

It’s a unique approach to melding distinct spirits categories and styles. And while many Westerners are still unfamiliar with baijiu, it’s generally considered the world’s largest spirits category, with annual sales almost double that of the global whiskey market. At the outset, Shang seems keen on targeting two separate consumer bases: baijiu-curious Americans, and existing baijiu drinkers searching for an injection of novelty.

Let’s dive in.

Shang Whiskey Dàn Ya Review

The baijiu used for Dàn Ya’s jiàngxiang whiskey begins with red sorghum in the Chìshui River basin. The sorghum base undergoes solid-state fermentation using dàqu, a starter that facilitates both saccharification and fermentation. Production follows a complex series of eight fermentations, separated by seven distillations. The distillate is rested in oxygen permeable clay pots for a minimum of three years. Finally, the baijiu is pot distilled and pressure filtered before shipping to Kentucky, where the resulting jiàngxiang whiskey is aged in American oak for between one month to “just under” a year.

On the nose, dedicated whiskey drinkers will likely encounter something quite new. Early aromas are at once tangy, sour, fruity, floral, and salty, somewhere between overripe tropical fruit and a savory fermented sauce or bean paste. Additional notes include bitter melon, lemongrass, pickled watermelon rind, and unsweetened chocolate. It’s certainly a broad mix, and it takes time to really parse the individual components. Oak develops later on, lending touches of vanilla and light caramel, which (eventually) push the nose into more familiar whiskey territory.

The palate starts with floral simple syrup and a big hit of red peppercorns, the latter dominating for a couple sips. After some acclimation comes loads more fruit, including tart berry compote, passionfruit, lychee, and pomelo. The back palate brings salinity and sweet/savory red bean paste, with lingering pepper. 100 proof.

B+ / $65 (500ml)

Shang Whiskey East + West Kentucky Blend Review

East + West starts with the jiàngxiang whiskey base and marries it with whiskey distilled from 100% red sorghum. That second component is produced at Whiskey House via sweet mash fermentation and grain-on column distillation up to 155 proof. (A Whiskey House representative confirmed the team used a relatively neutral yeast and enzymes similar to a high corn bourbon.) After the two components are blended, they undergo maturation in American oak barrels.

East + West kicks off with a profile far more familiar to whiskey drinkers. The nose begins with toasted oak and fermenting grain, and at first, it’s a little reminiscent of fermenting mash. Baking spice and chocolate are up next, and once again, it’s still firmly in whiskey territory: allspice, clove, and nutmeg meet hot cocoa. Eventually, some of the funky, ripe fruit character from Dàn Ya rolls in, along with a savory, peppery sauce (hoisin comes to mind).

The palate borrows a lot from Dàn Ya, with both pepper and tart fruit dialed back by around half. That allows for more caramel and milk chocolate, along with threads of bright red cherry and honeydew I didn’t pick up on the first expression. Similarly, the saline is toned down, and in its place we’ve got both pickled and candied ginger. The sweeter finish brings golden raisins and black pepper.

For American palates, East + West is less adventurous but more familiar. My guess is that could up the appeal stateside, though it reigns in some of what makes Dàn Ya intricate and fun. 92 proof.

B+ / $46 (500ml)

title: Review: Angostura Demerara Sugar Syrup and Spicy Honey Syrup
summary:
When it comes to cocktails, everyone knows Angostura for their iconic bitters. Now the brand is branching out into the cocktail syrup game with the introduction of their new Demerara Sugar Syrup and Spicy Honey Syrup. Cocktail syrups can be great for simplifying cocktail preparation at home, but they can also be tricky, sometimes packing…

The post Review: Angostura Demerara Sugar Syrup and Spicy Honey Syrup appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
When it comes to cocktails, everyone knows Angostura for their iconic bitters. Now the brand is branching out into the cocktail syrup game with the introduction of their new Demerara Sugar Syrup and Spicy Honey Syrup. Cocktail syrups can be great for simplifying cocktail preparation at home, but they can also be tricky, sometimes packing too much flavor and sweetness to the point that they overpower a standard base spirit. Let’s check out this duo from Angostura and see if they nailed the formulas out of the gate.

Angostura Demerara Sugar Syrup Review

The Demerara Sugar Syrup is the more versatile of the two, something you can use for almost any cocktail built around a barrel-aged spirit like whiskey or rum. It’s rich without being overly thick, delivering bold notes of overcooked caramel, molasses, and toffee that immediately distinguish it from standard simple syrup. But go easy because things can get overly saccharine fast if you’re not careful. Added sparingly, it contributes a nice mix of sweetness and texture to cocktails. The Old Fashioned recipe printed on the label is a good example, recommending half an ounce of syrup to two ounces of bourbon. If that bourbon is 100 proof or higher, you might be alright, but it’s simply too sweet with a standard 80-90 proof bottle. Start with a quarter of an ounce and work your way up, and the syrup adds that richness without overwhelming the whiskey. B+

Angostura Spicy Honey Syrup Review

The Spicy Honey Syrup is the more adventurous of the two, but also the more restrained when it comes to sweetness. Built on a foundation of floral honey, it layers warming baking spices, cinnamon, clove, and a touch of peppery heat into a syrup that feels equally suited to whiskey, rum, tequila, and even non-alcoholic cocktails. The spice isn’t overblown, but it does lend a noticeable, red chili warmth that lingers. It shines in a Gold Rush, a Hot Toddy, or, as Angostura recommends on the label, a spicy margarita. The honey softens the citrus and adds a silky texture while the spice infuses a gentle, complimenting heat. Another pro tip: you may need to look for added sweetness in other ingredients when using this syrup. Classic bourbons work well enough, but in a margarita, you’ll need a sweeter tequila (I’d use a reposado) or a dash of triple sec to achieve balance. B+

Like their iconic bitters, Angostura’s new syrups are no instant cocktail shortcut, but used thoughtfully and judiciously, they enhance all manner of drinks and should save bartenders, professional and novice alike, a few steps behind the bar.

$12 each (375ml)

summary:
When the Isle of Harris Distillery opened in 2015, it wasn’t simply launching another Scotch whisky brand. The post Island in a Bottle: Isle of Harris Distillery’s Shona Macleod appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
When the Isle of Harris Distillery opened in 2015, it wasn’t simply launching another Scotch whisky brand. It was attempting something far more ambitious: creating meaningful work in one of Scotland’s most remote communities and proving that world-class spirits could emerge from the edge of the Atlantic. There was just one issue. Almost no one involved had ever made spirits before.

The distillery’s original employees—known locally as the “Tarbert Ten”—came not from the whisky industry but from careers in construction and hospitality, among others. Together, they learned the craft of spirits production from the ground up, building both a distillery and a culture defined by curiosity and experimentation. That spirit of continual learning remains central to the Isle of Harris story today.

Few people embody that journey better than Shona Macleod. A member of the founding team, she joined as Guest Services Manager before discovering an unexpected talent for sensory analysis and blending, helping to make Isle of Harris Gin before shifting to whisky production and, in 2023, becoming official distillery blender. In her current role, she has guided the release of a line of young single malts including their newest addition, Isle of Harris Whisky.

In our conversation, Macleod discusses the challenges of distilling on a remote island, what makes Isle of Harris whiskies unique, and how a distillery founded to support the island’s community is now working with other Hebridean distilleries to bring that region’s unique whiskies to the world.

Note: This interview has been edited for clarity.

Drinkhacker: What is your background in spirits production? How did you become the official blender at the Isle of Harris Distillery?

Macleod: In December 2014, I joined the distillery as part of the “Tarbert Ten” and began my journey as Guest Services Manager. Our original small team were all involved in gin quality from the very beginning and we were tested to check if we had good sensory skills. It had never crossed my mind that I did or that it would be something I would enjoy but I did!  My involvement in the sensory and quality aspects of Isle of Harris Gin then naturally sparked a deep interest in whisky production and flavour profiles in both new make spirit and maturing whisky.

As we moved closer to launching our first whisky, we needed more in-house expertise in sensory work and blending, so I began a new chapter within the production team.   Learning the craft and science of distillation, maturation, and cask selection has been a huge learning curve for me.  Every day brings new opportunities, challenges, and the joy of creating something that reflects our island home.

Drinkhacker: I’ve read that there is an “always learning” mindset at the distillery. How has that been applied in your whisky-making?

Macleod: It’s quite an appropriate phrase when it comes to our whisky making as the distillery is only 10 years old, and we were all new to whisky making when we started out. The purpose of the distillery was to create jobs locally, as such, the company had to recruit people who lived on the island. With no history of distilling here in Harris, these roles were filled by a group of people who had no previous experience in the whisky industry. Our original distillers came from different backgrounds such as facilities management, engineering and the building trade. It was a big learning curve for all involved so we are always learning!

Drinkhacker: How has the distillery supported the broader community on Isle of Harris?

Macleod: The purpose of the distillery extends beyond making whisky and gin. Primarily by providing employment and career development opportunities in a small community and sustaining many families. It has helped keep some young locals on the island who may have gone elsewhere to follow a career path. Instead, they found interesting opportunities here. To others like myself with no experience in the whisky industry, it offered a new challenge and something for us to be proud of. The ability for many of us to live and work at home in Harris has had a really positive economic impact on the island.

More broadly, the aim was also to help boost tourism and be a catalyst for other small businesses to develop and make Harris a better destination for visitors. We have welcomed over 650,000 visitors through our doors since opening in September 2015 which is quite exceptional.

Drinkhacker: What are some of the challenges of producing single malt whisky on an island like Harris?

Macleod: Building a new business in a remote location is a challenge in itself in terms of logistics, infrastructure and added costs for almost everything.  From finding a suitable site with a fresh water source nearby through to the construction phase and all the challenges that brought wasn’t easy by any means. Specialist firms had to be used to construct the distilling plant, and the ongoing maintenance is costly as people have to travel from the mainland and stay over when work is being carried out if it can’t be handled locally. We rely on ferries to take all our raw materials in and finished goods away which can be challenging when we’re at the mercy of the Hebridean weather! We’re no strangers to shifting schedules and thinking on our feet.

Drinkhacker: How would you describe the Isle of Harris house whisky style? What sets it apart from whiskies from other regions of Scotland?

Macleod: It’s unique because it’s the first whisky from the Isle of Harris, at least the first legal one. I’m sure there were illicit stills many years ago! We set up our production processes to produce a certain type of new make spirit, one that was light and fruity and quick to mature but as no one had produced whisky commercially here before, we didn’t know how long it might take to be at its best, ready for release. Happily, we discovered that the maturation conditions are excellent at our warehouses on the shores of the Atlantic and within five years we had a good idea that we had something special.

In terms of style, there isn’t a ‘Hebridean’ style as such, so we weren’t aiming to produce a whisky that was particularly like any other in flavour profile. Instead, we set out to create a dram of distinction, fruity, floral and spiced with just a touch of smoke. The most important thing was that it was complex and full of character, just like the people making it.

Drinkhacker: What is unique about your production process?

Macleod: Our process is not hurried by time, everything is fairly slow such as the mash, the fermentations and the distillation time. Our distillers are involved with every part of the process, it’s not automated so they manually adjust steam valves and the cut point is made using sight and nosing skills. I think the human touch influences the character and quality of the spirit and importantly gives them real skills in the art of distilling that they might not have learnt in a larger distillery.

Drinkhacker: What is wood management like on the island? How did you settle on oloroso and Fino in addition to ex-bourbon for aging your whiskies?
Macleod: Cask availability is much the same as anywhere else, they just have to travel a little further to reach us! Some from Kentucky and some from Southern Spain. Our casks are delivered straight into the yard at the distillery, next to the shore at East Loch Tarbert where they sit until they’re filled before being sent to the maturation warehouses, 2 miles from the distillery. I’ve no doubt the proximity to the sea prior to filling helps add a maritime character to the whisky as it ages.

The original cask mix of ex bourbon barrels from Buffalo Trace, Heaven Hill and Woodford Reserve, plus ex oloroso casks was decided on during the development phase when we had experienced consultants to help with recipes and production processes. Fino came a little later as a bit of an experiment, but we discovered that Fino casks mature our spirit really well in this climate.  In addition to our core cask portfolio, we have a small number of sweet wine casks from our friends at Chateau Biac in Bordeaux, Pennsylvanian Rye casks from Dad’s Hat Distillery, Pedro Ximenez, Palo Cortado and Orange Wine casks from our Spanish supplier, Yose y Miguel Martin in Heulva.

Drinkhacker: What is the maturation climate like on the island?

Macleod: We have quite stable temperatures through the year in The Hebrides, it never gets too hot or too cold which is an ideal atmosphere for whisky maturation.  The Island is directly on the Atlantic so there is always a lot of moisture in the air from frequent rainfall and sea mist, this humidity seems to aid maturation. It’s often very windy where the warehouses are located. This can encourage the angels share to disappear a little quicker, but it produces some great whisky in a relatively short period of time.

Drinkhacker: Other distilleries are following your lead in the Outer Hebrides. Are you working together?

Macleod: In 2018 we began to develop “The Hebridean Whisky Trail” with neighboring distilleries on the Isle of Skye – Raasay, Torabhaig and Talisker. Our aim was to put a spotlight on this part of The Hebrides as a whisky destination and a producer of world class spirits. With three of the four of us being new (Talisker pre-dated the rest of us by about 180 years!) it was always hoped that other Outer Hebridean Distilleries would emerge which they did in the years that followed. On the neighbouring island of Benbecula, North Uist Distillery and Benbecula Distillery have been established and joined the trail. It’s been fantastic to see new distilleries open up close by and welcomed with open arms. In addition, our friends from Tiree Distillery and Tobermory have also joined. Each year we have our own Hebridean Whisky Festival in September involving all the distilleries which continues to grow from strength to strength. Perhaps we’ll be granted an official region title one day, that’s our hope.


Drinkhacker: How does the new Isle of Harris Whisky fit into the brand’s portfolio?

Macleod: It represents a natural next step for the distillery, moving from a single flagship whisky to a broader range and builds our portfolio. With more maturing stock available, It’s an evolution rather than a change of direction. We want this dram to be seen as one to enjoy with friends and family rather than being viewed as a collectible whisky or one saved for special occasions. It’s really versatile so it can be enjoyed as a traditional straight dram or used in highballs and cocktails. Please try it and let me know what you think!

Drinkhacker: After a decade of whisky-making, what are you most proud of?

Macleod: I’m very proud to see the growth that the distillery has enjoyed and how much we’ve achieved in the past 10 years. Building an international award-winning brand from our small island in the Outer Hebrides, creating skilled jobs and marking our place in the history books are highlights for me personally.  The success of Isle of Harris Gin is ongoing and to now have three core whiskies on the market that we are truly proud of is a real milestone for us.

Drinkhacker: What will the distillery look like in another decade? What do you hope to achieve going forward?

Macleod: No one knows what the future holds, but we’ll strive to continue to produce world class spirits from Harris and look forward to continued growth. To build on the success of the first 10 years and to always remember the vision that our founder Anderson Bakewell had in those early years when he wondered to himself “how can we bottle the essence of this beautiful island and share it with the world”.

content:
When we last visited Glenglassaugh’s core range in 2023, the final scores threw a curveball. The distillery’s 12 year old single malt — the line’s only age-stated whisky — lagged behind the NAS bottlings. (We also reviewed a 46 year from before the distillery’s 1986 shuttering, which is a different and altogether great whisky.) But 2026 brings a range expansion, and with it, a chance to reassess. Glenglassaugh 15 Years Old is the newest permanent expression from the Highlands distillery, and the first to leverage Pedro Ximénez sherry for aging.

Blending was overseen by Dr. Rachel Barrie, who serves as Master Blender for Glenglassaugh and sister distilleries Glendronach and Benriach. (All three are owned by Louisville-based Brown-Forman.) The whisky was aged across both PX sherry and Spanish wine casks, which Barries says adds an “indulgent depth of flavor” to Glenglassaugh’s typically coastal and fruity profile.

Let’s dive in.

Glenglassaugh 15 Years Old Review

Pedro Ximénez influence is front and center on the nose, with alternating waves of dates, brandied cherries, and black raisins. Burnt orange peel lends a touch of citrus, but it pales in comparison to those dark, dried fruits. A dry nuttiness is up next, closest to black walnut, along with a less pronounced thread of toasted sesame oil. Toffee, roasted coffee beans, and cocoa powder round out a nose reminiscent of whiskies from sister distillery Glendronach — and quite unlike any other whiskies in the standard Glenglassaugh lineup.

Based on the nose, I was worried the 15 year’s palate could turn into a sherry bomb. Fortunately, that influence is a tad less declarative here, allowing the distillate itself to shine on first sips. Hallmark tropical and orchard fruits hit early, including guava, apple juice, and very ripe papaya, drizzled with a dark syrup or treacle. Overall, the fruits aren’t quite as bright as with some other Glenglassaugh malts (like Sandend), and they’re tempered by PX and oxidized wine; still, the end result is a pleasantly sweet, somewhat richer medley. Chocolate arrives only at and beyond the midpalate, far lighter than the nose, along with tart marmalade.

The finish gradually transitions from fruit, treacle, and chocolate to sweetened espresso. (A nice Café Cubano, if you want to get fancy.) A touch of lingering salinity continues for well over a minute after each sip — appropriate for a famously coastal aging setup.

It’s a nice bookend to the narrative, one that very much feels like Glenglassaugh through the eyes of Rachel Barrie. I’ll admit that when I first heard the whisky’s specs — specifically the use of Pedro Ximénez — I was a bit skeptical. But Barrie lands the plane. Glenglassaugh 15 Years Old improves on the distillery’s 12 year bottling by tempering the graininess and introducing significantly more depth from the casks. Fingers crossed we see more in this direction.

92 proof.

A- / $110

The post Tasting Report: Spotlight on 2026 Italian Wine Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We didn’t make it to Wine Paris this year, but Wine Paris made it to us, courtesy of Communicare il Vino, which sent along 12 selections from its Italian portfolio which were showcased at the event. These hail from all over Italy, and we’re breaking them down by broad category, then order of preference.

Sparkling

2025 Sant’Anna dei Bricchetti Vino Spumante Incanto Pas Dosè – Rather dry and initially innocuous, the wine opens up with time to reveal a core of lemon and melon, though it’s all rather buried under a heavy layer of doughy yeast. An initially intense fizz takes some time to settle down, but it takes a lot of that fruit with it. B / $17

Whites

2023 Rosset Petite Arvine Valle d’Aoste – Petite arvine is a white grape varietal designed to thrive in cold climates. This unoaked offering showcases a mix of honeysuckle and fresh fruit, namely apple and aromatic pear notes, with touches of Meyer lemon. Lightly perfumed as the finish builds, notes of sandalwood give it a slightly smoldering vibe that hints at incense. Outstanding as an aperitif. A- / $35

2022 Querceto di Castellina Livia IGT – A quirky blend of viognier and roussanne, two grapes I rarely associate with Italy at all. The more Rhone-leaning side of this blend dominates here, offering a floral-herbal character that emerges as quite dry and pastoral. Elements of hay and lemongrass give the finish a massive length, but one that plays in the forest and the dust, merely tiptoeing into the orchard to grab a fig or an apricot from time to time. B+ / $45

2024 La Regola Steccaia IGT – Vermentino doesn’t often acquit itself as this gentle and supple, layers of nougat and pastry cream evoking notes of melon, covered in white flowers. A sharper, zippier note hints at the heavy acidity that vermentino is so well-known for, but it never breaks out of its more undulating groove, concluding on notes of coconut cream. A light grind of lemon peel across the top finishes things out on a lighter note. B+ / $40

Reds

2023 Sassotondo Monte Calvo Ciliegiolo – There are a few Monte Calvos in Italy; this one is a small volcano in Tuscany’s Maremma region, where ciliegiolo grapes (purportedly a progenitor of sangiovese, though this is disputed) grow in the volcanic soil. Aged in large barrels for a year, this wine is a delight. Light on its feet, this effortless expression of the grape showcases cherry fruit at its brightest and most maraschino-like, gently sweet and layered with light notes of almond syrup, red flowers, and a pinch of peppery spice. Its flavors are beautifully integrated from start to finish, culminating in a seductive creaminess you don’t often find in a wine the light in body. Delightful. A / $45

2024 San Gregorio Chianti Colli Senesi (pictured) – Bright berries kick things off with a rush of cherry, followed by some surprising blueberry notes, all swirled together with cinnamon syrup. Light notes of graphite and tar add just enough tannic gravity to the wine, which finishes a bit on the tart side with a punch of fresh cranberry juice. This gentle sourness becomes more insistent as the wine fades, but it maintains a lively balance throughout that invites repeated visits. A shockingly good value. A / $15

2021 Ricordi Sant’Anna dei Bricchetti Barbera d’Asti DOCG – A bolder and denser barbera than you’re likely to encounter in the wild, this is a rich and more fruit-forward experience that shocks as it evokes barbera’s big brother grapes far more than expected. Unctuous notes of plum and cherry meld with black tea and bittersweet chocolate, but ample acidity linger throughout the experience — well into the finish. Tart boysenberry and spice elements give the conclusion a holiday feel that, again, doesn’t connect with the classic barbera experience — but which isn’t at all unwelcome. A- / $10

2021 Capezzana Ghiaie della Furba IGT – An unusual super Tuscan blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, and Merlot, this is one of the more intense and brooding wines I’ve encountered in recent memory, overloaded with tar and turned earth, punctuated throughout with anise. Dark chocolate, coffee bean, and blackstrap molasses notes meld fitfully as the palate develops, culminating in rich, impossibly black fruit overtones that somehow get more intense as the wine develops. Let this monster linger in the cellar for another decade and you are likely to be rewarded with a lithe experience that shows Tuscany at the top of its game. Ands yet, surprisingly, it’s still approachable now, as long as you are prepared for what you’re getting in to. A- / $70

2021 Monchiero Barolo Rocche di Castiglione DOCG – Amazingly floral on the nose, infused with roses that telegraph where this wine might end up, but the palate is tight as a fist for now. Airtime or decanting is a help, tempering tannins and the more balsamic elements of the wine, revealing a layer of turned earth waiting underneath. Bright cherry emerges after that, although slightly underripe, a further sign of how many years this wine has ahead of it. There’s joy to be had now with ample patience, but I’d likely try it again around 2031. B+/ $64

2019 Pardi Montefalco Rosso Riserva DOC – Intense cherry backed with rhubarb kicks things off on this intense yet approachable wine, which fades slowly into notes of plum, bittersweet chocolate, and rum raisin elements. Brooding with green herbs and turned earth as the finish approaches, a slightly leathery character awaits as the finish approaches. The experience remains tart to an extreme, with licks of anise ringing the edges of the wine. Ideally paired with a lively dinner. B+ / $27

2018 Antonelli Chiusa di Pannone Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG – A well-aged sagrantino, this wine hits hard with notes of raisin and dried currants, increasingly tarry as it develops in glass. The tannins remain firm to the point of being nearly overbearing, giving the back end a heavy character of tar and asphalt, somewhat bitter at times. The finish echoes blackberry and prune notes, with dark chocolate making a brief appearance. Though aggressive, this could be an interesting choice today with the right meal pairing, but something that probably needs 5 to 10 more years in cellar to develop. B+ / $57

2022 Castello La Leccia Chianti Classico – Quite dry on the attack, with a balsamic edge and overtones of turned earth, anise, and late-stage basil. Graphite and slate inform an enduringly bone-dry palate that sees some dried florals developing but which never quite come to fruition. Cherry fruit on the finish is rather underripe, laced with tar and pencil lead. B / $20

content:
Rare Character Whiskey launched in 2021, founded by spirits industry veterans Pablo Moix and Peter Nevenglosky. The independent bottler quickly developed a devoted following by focusing on single barrel selections, custom labels, and premium whiskey stocks. It also became closely associated with its barrel code system, with certain codes developing dedicated followings and becoming highly collectible.

In the spring of 2023, Rare Character temporarily shifted its focus away from barrel code branding for Pride of Anderson County Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey. The original release left little room for speculation about its origin. The back label identified Wild Turkey Distilling in Lawrenceburg, Kentucky, as the source of the bourbon while also specifying the rickhouse and floor where each barrel matured. It even referenced Tyrone, Kentucky, the small unincorporated riverfront community in Anderson County located roughly three miles from Lawrenceburg and generally regarded as the more precise location of Wild Turkey. Enthusiasm surrounding the inaugural release was considerable, and bottles quickly became difficult to obtain.

Three years later, Rare Character introduced the next chapter for Pride of Anderson County. The brand shifted from a lottery-exclusive release to an ongoing single barrel series. Although the name remains Pride of Anderson County, the back label received a significant overhaul. The 2026 version omits any reference to Wild Turkey, its rickhouses, individual warehouse floors, or Tyrone.

Rare Character was unable to comment on the source of the 2026 iterations of Pride of Anderson County due to non-disclosure agreements. Even so, the origins of the brand remain closely tied to Wild Turkey, and Anderson County is home to the distillery. With almost full certainty, Pride of Anderson County continues to be distilled by Wild Turkey from a mashbill of 75% corn, 13% rye, and 12% malted barley, using entirely non-GMO grains. Pride of Anderson County is aged for at least nine years in barrels with a #4 alligator char and entered into the barrel at 115 proof after the distillate exits the column still at 125 proof and the doubler at 128 proof.

Rare Character provided Drinkhacker with a review sample aged for at least 9.5 years, making it several years younger than the 13.5 year-old bourbon released in 2023. According to Rare Character, Pride of Anderson County is intended as “a tribute to legends… both past and present.”

Does the liquid live up to the legend?

Pride of Anderson County Bourbon 9.5 Years Old Review

The nose opens with an artificial vanilla taffy note that arrives with plenty of intensity but disappears almost as quickly as it appears. From there, dried cherries and sweetened cocoa powder take over, while roasted pecans arrive later to provide a sturdy foundation along with a touch of tannic dryness. Aside from that fleeting vanilla note at the start, the bouquet lands squarely in classic bourbon territory.

The palate begins with sweet apple jelly before shifting into a potent, short-lived sour cherry note. That quickly transforms into cherry cola, accompanied by a medium-thick mouthfeel. The finish keeps the cherry theme going with cherry preserves and dark brown sugar. That darker sweetness transitions into a smidge of sweet and nutty late-harvest dark maple syrup before closing with sweet cinnamon chewing gum.

This is a fun bourbon. Beyond the opening aroma of artificial vanilla, Pride of Anderson County delivers on nearly every front. For anyone seeking a bourbon driven by cherry, this bottle fits the bill. I cannot recall another bourbon that explores so many different expressions of cherry within a single pour, and I enjoyed every minute of that ride. With that said, as much as I enjoyed this bourbon, the asking price of $250 is a tall ask. If this specific barrel were priced in the range of $150, I’d be all in.

119.8 proof.

A / $250
